Evidence B:026 explicitly describes fabrication behavior as a "critical limitation," and A:034/A:007 similarly conclude agents "cannot yet automate tasks for data-driven discovery." However, the type confidence is moderate because the specific failure modes differ (low success rate vs. fabrication of results), and there is no citation link between the papers, making this a convergent but not directly corroborating relationship.

Both contributions construct benchmark datasets for evaluating LLM-based scientific hypothesis generation, addressing the same high-level research question. However, their designs are fundamentally different: Contribution A (MOOSE-Chem) builds a benchmark of 51 chemistry papers manually decomposed by PhD chemists into background/inspirations/hypothesis, specifically targeting contamination-free evaluation using papers published after LLM training cutoffs (A:002, A:006). Contribution B (KG-CoI) constructs a dataset by masking edges in a biomedical knowledge graph (PubTator3) and asking LLMs to predict withheld relations, enabling quantitative ground-truth comparison (B:004, B:018). There is no citation between the papers and no evidence that either explicitly builds on, refines, or contradicts the other. The shared topic of LLM hypothesis generation benchmarking establishes a substantive relationship, but the methodological approaches, domains (chemistry vs. biomedical KG), and benchmark construction strategies are distinct enough that no hard semantic relation type (supports, builds_on, refines, contradicts) is defensible from the evidence alone.

Both contributions independently construct benchmark datasets from 2024 journal publications specifically to enable contamination-free evaluation of LLM-based scientific hypothesis generation beyond model pretraining cutoffs. Contribution A (51 chemistry/materials papers from Nature/Science-level venues, decomposed into background/inspirations/hypothesis) and Contribution B (MATDESIGN, ~50 materials-discovery papers with goals, constraints, and ground-truth materials/methods) converge on the same core finding: that post-cutoff benchmarks grounded in real publications are necessary and feasible for evaluating LLM hypothesis generation. B:001 and B:008 explicitly frame MATDESIGN as addressing the same contamination concern, and both benchmarks share the structural choice of sourcing from 2024 publications. There is no citation between the papers, no explicit reuse of methods or artifacts (ruling out builds_on/refines), and no incompatible findings (ruling out contradicts). The parallel design choices and shared conclusions constitute materially corroborating findings, supporting a 'supports' (symmetric) classification, though the moderate type confidence reflects that the benchmarks differ in domain focus (general chemistry hypothesis vs. materials-design constraints) and evaluation framing.

Both contributions address the same high-level problem—evaluating LLMs' ability to generate scientific hypotheses—and both construct benchmark datasets for this purpose. Contribution A (MOOSE-Chem) builds a 51-paper chemistry benchmark from Nature/Science papers and tests rediscovery without data contamination (AQ, A:002, A:006). Contribution B (KG-CoI) constructs a 300-instance biomedical benchmark by masking KG edges and evaluating LLMs' ability to hypothesize withheld relations (BQ, B:001, B:018, B:038). The two works share the same research theme and comparable methodology (benchmark construction + LLM evaluation), but differ substantially in domain (chemistry vs. biomedicine), benchmark construction approach (annotated papers vs. KG edge masking), and technical method (multi-agent agentic framework vs. KG-augmented chain-of-ideas). There is no citation between the papers and no evidence that either explicitly uses, extends, or corrects the other's artifacts or findings. The relationship is substantive enough to be more than 'none', but the evidence does not support a hard 'supports', 'builds_on', or 'refines' classification.

Both contributions converge on the same core finding: LLMs can be productively used as generators of novel scientific hypotheses. Contribution A shows empirically that an LLM-based framework can rediscover high-quality chemistry hypotheses published in Nature and Science without data contamination (AQ, A:002, A:032). Contribution B argues and experimentally demonstrates that LLM "hallucinations" — probabilistic outputs beyond strict inference — can be harnessed as a source of novel, testable scientific hypotheses in the domain of breast cancer treatment (BQ, B:001, B:006). Both findings corroborate the broader claim that LLMs are viable tools for scientific hypothesis generation, with empirical results in complementary domains (chemistry vs. biomedicine). However, the two contributions approach the same space from different angles (rediscovery benchmark vs. experimental validation of hallucination-derived hypotheses) and do not explicitly cite or build on each other, keeping the relation at 'supports' rather than 'builds_on'. The absence of any citation between them and the distinct methodological framings prevent a stronger hard type.

Both contributions independently demonstrate that LLM-based frameworks can generate research ideas of high quality—Contribution A shows LLMs can rediscover chemistry hypotheses at Nature/Science level (AQ, A:002), while Contribution B shows LLM-generated astronomy ideas achieve novelty scores of 3+/6 and match or exceed human-generated ideas (BQ). However, there is no citation between the papers and no explicit cross-reference, so the support is inferential rather than direct. The relation is symmetric supports, but confidence in type is moderate given domain differences and the absence of a direct cross-citation.

Both contributions address LLM-based scientific hypothesis generation and share topical overlap: Contribution A (MOOSE-Chem) proposes that LLMs encode latent knowledge associations enabling novel hypothesis generation, evidenced by out-of-distribution inspiration retrieval accuracy [AQ, A:003], and constructs a benchmark of 51 chemistry papers for evaluation [A:006]. Both contributions share a core compatible finding: LLMs encode latent knowledge that can be productively exploited for novel scientific hypothesis generation beyond what human scientists have explicitly recognized. Contribution A argues that LLMs already encode latent knowledge associations enabling novel hypothesis generation (evidenced by out-of-distribution inspiration retrieval accuracy; AQ, A:003, A:018), while Contribution B argues that LLM hallucinations — probabilistic deviations — can serve as a productive source of novel, testable scientific hypotheses (BQ, B:001). There is no citation link between the papers, and neither explicitly uses or extends the other's method or artifact. The shared positive empirical stance on LLMs as hypothesis generators constitutes a mutual corroboration (supports), though the mechanistic framing differs enough to limit confidence in type classification over 'related'.

Both contributions make corroborating claims about LLMs' latent capacity for scientific discovery: A argues LLMs encode latent knowledge associations enabling novel hypothesis generation (evidenced by out-of-distribution inspiration retrieval), while B shows LLMs can generate relevant, novel, feasible research ideas across disciplines. The support relation is defensible but moderate, as the contributions address related but distinct aspects of LLM scientific discovery capability without directly measuring the same construct.

Both contributions address the same research problem — evaluating LLMs' scientific idea generation capabilities — but do so with fundamentally different methodological designs. The relationship is substantive and topically tight but does not rise to a defensible 'supports', 'builds_on', or 'contradicts' classification without stronger evidence of direct connection.

A cites B as a prior autonomous research agent system (ResearchAgent), listing it in a comparison table of evaluation protocols. Both contributions address the same overarching question — evaluating LLM-generated research ideas — but from distinct angles and with independent methodologies. A:008 notes that LLM ideas "lack idea diversity when we scale up idea generation," which is precisely the gap IDI addresses, but this is not a direct build-on relationship since A does not use IDI and B does not cite A. The relationship is therefore substantive but not classifiable as a hard builds_on, refines, supports, or contradicts without overreaching the evidence.

Both contributions address the same research question: how LLM-generated scientific ideas compare to human expert ideas, and how automated evaluation aligns with expert judgment in that context. The relationship is substantive (both probe LLM ideation quality and the human vs. automated evaluation gap) but the hard type cannot be confidently established as 'refines' or 'builds_on' without explicit methodological reuse. 'Related' is the most defensible classification.

Both contributions concern characterizing LLM capabilities and limitations—Contribution A identifies lack of diversity and unreliable self-evaluation as failure modes in LLM ideation agents, while Contribution B proposes a framework for characterizing LLMs as probabilistic imperfect experts along dimensions including reliability and consistency. Both contributions investigate LLM capabilities for scientific idea generation and share overlapping concerns about systematic limitations of LLMs in this domain. The relationship is substantive but does not rise to a defensible hard type (supports, builds_on, refines, or contradicts), making "related" the most appropriate classification.

Both contributions address the same problem — improving LLM-generated research idea novelty using retrieval-augmented generation and inference-time scaling — and operate in overlapping territory. Contribution B (Nova) explicitly references Contribution A ("AI-Researcher" by Si et al., 2024) in its comparison table [B:001], listing it as a baseline and distinguishing Nova's planning-guided RAG from A's approach. However, B does not directly build on A's methods or extend its artifacts; rather, it proposes an independent framework and benchmarks against A. Contribution A identifies a bottleneck in overgenerate-and-rerank (idea diversity plateaus at ~200 unique ideas from 4000 [A:036]), which is precisely the problem B's planning-guided retrieval is designed to address [B:004, BQ], suggesting B's approach could be seen as refining or responding to A's findings. Yet there is no citation between the papers in the resolved corpus, and B does not explicitly frame itself as correcting or extending A's specific methodology — it cites it only as a baseline comparison. The relationship is substantive (same domain, overlapping methods, B cites A as a baseline) but the evidence is insufficient to confidently classify it as builds_on or refines rather than a strong related relationship.

Both contributions address evaluation of LLM-generated scientific ideas, specifically the gap between automated/LLM-as-judge assessments and human expert judgments. Contribution A (Si et al.) proposes an end-to-end study design in which recruited researchers execute generated ideas into full projects to determine whether expert novelty/feasibility judgments translate to real research outcomes [A:003, AQ]. Contribution B quantifies the systematic discrepancy between LLM-as-judge scores and PhD-level expert ratings (r=0.02–0.17, 3–4 point gap on a 10-point scale), arguing that automated scores reflect relative architectural differences rather than absolute quality [B:003, B:007, BQ]. Both contributions are substantively concerned with the validity and reliability of evaluation protocols for scientific ideation—A by proposing outcome-based ground truth, B by empirically measuring the automated-vs-expert divergence. However, there is no citation between the papers, B does not explicitly build on or extend A's method or artifact, and the findings are complementary rather than directly corroborating or contradicting the same construct. The relationship is substantive (both diagnose the evaluation validity problem from different angles) but no hard directional type (builds_on, refines, supports, contradicts) is clearly defensible from the evidence alone.

Both contributions introduce benchmarks for evaluating AI agents on scientific research tasks derived from real-world research papers — CORE-Bench (A) targets computational reproducibility across CS, social science, and medicine with 270 tasks, while Curie's benchmark (B) targets scientific experimentation across four CS domains with 46 tasks. Both contributions address the same problem space — automated LLM-based academic peer review — but from complementary angles: Contribution A (CycleReviewer) is an operational reward model trained to simulate peer review and evaluated on score prediction accuracy (MAE), while Contribution B (MMReview) is a comprehensive evaluation benchmark designed to rigorously assess LLM-based review systems across disciplines and modalities. Both contributions address the frontier of automated scientific research using LLMs — Contribution A (CycleReviewer) focuses on automated peer review as a reward model within a full research automation loop, while Contribution B (The AI Scientist) focuses on end-to-end automated manuscript generation that passes human peer review. Both contributions address the same core problem — reducing hallucinations in LLM-based scientific hypothesis generation by grounding outputs in structured/formal knowledge — and arrive at convergent findings. Contribution A (KG-CoI) demonstrates that linking LLM hypothesis generation to knowledge graphs reduces hallucinations and improves accuracy (A:001, A:004, A:005). Contribution B independently demonstrates that combining inductive logic programming, LLMs, and rigorous ontologies grounded in community databases likewise mitigates hallucinations while preserving language-driven flexibility (B:000, B:001, B:006, BQ). The shared finding — that anchoring LLMs to external structured/formal knowledge reduces hallucination in scientific hypothesis generation — constitutes mutually corroborating evidence. However, the approaches differ substantially (KG retrieval + chain-of-ideas vs. ILP + ontologies + lab automation), neither paper cites the other, and there is no explicit methodological dependency, so 'supports' (symmetric corroboration) is the most defensible relation rather than a harder directional type. Confidence is moderate because the topical overlap is strong but the specific experimental domains (general scientific KGs vs. yeast systems biology) diverge considerably.

Both contributions independently develop LLM-based scientific ideation systems that organize reasoning as a "chain of ideas" (CoI) structure. KG-CoI (A) explicitly adopts the "chain of ideas" framing and terminology for hypothesis generation, while CoI Agent (B) is the named originator of the Chain-of-Ideas concept for research ideation. This strongly suggests A builds on or is at least inspired by the CoI concept introduced by B. However, there is no citation between the papers in the resolved corpus, and A's evidence does not explicitly reference B's work — A cites other prior work (e.g., Wei et al. 2022 for chain-of-thought, SciMON, Zhou et al.) but not B. B's related work section (B:002) also does not cite A. The shared "chain of ideas" terminology and structural similarity (organizing LLM outputs chronologically/progressively as linked ideas) is substantive and goes beyond mere topical overlap, but without an explicit citation or methodological acknowledgment, a hard "builds_on" classification is not defensible. The relationship is best characterized as related — a substantive conceptual overlap and likely parallel or derivative development of the same core idea, but insufficiently evidenced for a harder relation type.

Both contributions are benchmark datasets specifically designed to evaluate LLM hypothesis generation, sharing the same high-level goal and task framing. Contribution A constructs a biomedical benchmark by masking links in a knowledge graph (PubTator3) to produce quantifiable ground-truth comparisons across LLMs (AQ, A:004, A:018). Contribution B constructs MATDESIGN, a materials-science benchmark drawn from 2024 journal publications to test LLMs beyond their pretraining cutoffs under real-world constraints (BQ, B:001, B:008). There is no citation between the papers, no evidence that one builds directly on the other's methods or artifacts, and no contradictory findings — they operate in different scientific domains (biomedical vs. materials science) with different construction strategies. However, the substantive topical parallel — parallel benchmark constructions for LLM hypothesis-generation evaluation — establishes a meaningful contribution-level relationship that warrants 'related' rather than 'none'.

Both contributions address the same problem — benchmarking hypothesis generation with LLMs — and share the core idea of constructing datasets to enable quantitative evaluation of LLM hypothesis generation methods. Contribution A builds a 300-instance dataset by masking KG relations and evaluating LLMs on recovering them, while Contribution B (HypoBench) constructs a far larger and more systematic benchmark (194 datasets, 7 real-world + 5 synthetic tasks) evaluating along three dimensions (practical utility, generalizability, ground-truth discovery rate). There is no citation between these papers, no evidence that either explicitly builds on or uses the other's artifacts, and no contradictory findings on the same construct. The shared focus on LLM hypothesis generation benchmarking makes this a substantive topical relationship, but the differences in scope, methodology, and framing (KG-masked-link recovery vs. data-driven pattern discovery) prevent a hard 'supports' or 'builds_on' classification. 'Related' best captures the substantive but non-specific connection.

Both contributions operate in the shared space of LLM-based scientific hypothesis generation and engage directly with the concept of hallucinations, but they take diametrically opposed stances on hallucinations rather than corroborating or building on each other. Contribution A treats hallucinations as a defect to be detected and suppressed via KG-grounded verification (A:001, A:005, AQ), while Contribution B reframes hallucinations as a productive resource for generating testable scientific hypotheses (BQ, B:001, B:006). This is a substantive thematic relationship — both address the same phenomenon (LLM hallucinations in scientific hypothesis generation) and reach contrasting but not strictly incompatible conclusions (mitigation vs. exploitation). However, the divergence is more of a complementary framing difference than a genuine empirical contradiction over the same measured construct, and there is no citation link or explicit engagement between the papers. A 'contradicts' classification would require them to be measuring the same outcome and reaching incompatible findings; instead they adopt different normative stances on hallucinations in different operational contexts. 'Related' is therefore the most defensible classification.

Both contributions address the same core problem—hallucination reduction in LLM-driven scientific hypothesis generation—and arrive at comparable findings: grounding LLM outputs in structured/relational knowledge (KGs, ontologies, relational databases, ILP) materially reduces hallucinations while preserving generative flexibility (A:001, A:005, B:001, B:003, B:006, BQ). However, the two systems are architecturally distinct (KG-CoI's chain-of-ideas verification vs. ILP+LLM+ontology pipeline), neither paper cites the other, and no evidence shows one explicitly builds on or refines the other's methods or results. The shared finding that structured knowledge grounding curbs hallucinations in scientific LLM outputs constitutes a 'supports' relationship, but the lack of citation and methodological independence keeps confidence moderate. 'Builds_on' or 'refines' are not defensible without evidence of direct use or extension of the other's artifact.

Both contributions share the same architectural paradigm — modular, multi-agent LLM-powered frameworks designed to automate scientific research workflows end-to-end — and both are situated within the AI-for-Science / self-driving-lab space. Baby-AIGS (A) targets autonomous, domain-agnostic scientific discovery across hypothesis proposal, experimentation, review, and falsification, while AILA (B) targets a specific physical laboratory instrument (AFM) with specialized hardware-control and data-analysis agents. The relationship is therefore substantive (shared problem framing, analogous architectural choices) but does not rise to the level of a defensible hard relation such as builds_on, refines, supports, or contradicts.

Both contributions share a core intellectual concern — using Popperian falsification principles within LLM-agent frameworks to validate or discover scientific hypotheses — making a substantive relationship clear. Contribution B (POPPER) cites Contribution A (BABY-AIGS/FalsificationAgent), and B:009 groups it with other systems that "integrate hypothesis and code generation" but "often lack strong error control," explicitly distinguishing POPPER from them. This suggests POPPER is aware of FalsificationAgent but positions itself as a distinct, statistically rigorous alternative rather than directly building on or refining it. The key differences are significant: FalsificationAgent operates within a full end-to-end AI research pipeline (BABY-AIGS) targeting discovery, while POPPER targets validation of free-form natural language hypotheses with formal sequential testing and strict Type-I error control. There is no evidence that POPPER reuses FalsificationAgent's methods, artifacts, or results (ruling out builds_on/refines), and their findings are not incompatible (ruling out contradicts). The citation in B:009 is used for background contrast rather than direct methodological extension. A 'related' classification best captures the shared falsification theme and mutual awareness without a defensible hard semantic type.

Both contributions are grounded in Popperian falsification and employ LLM agents to design and execute falsification experiments, establishing a clear topical and conceptual relationship. The shared falsification theme and the citation make a 'related' classification the most defensible: a substantive conceptual relationship exists (both tackle automated scientific falsification via LLM agents), but no hard directional semantic relation such as builds_on or refines is supported by the available evidence.

Both contributions address the same high-level problem — end-to-end agentic automated scientific discovery — and share overlapping design goals (autonomous hypothesis formulation, experiment execution, manuscript generation). The relationship is substantive but only at the level of shared domain and complementary design choices, making 'related' the most defensible classification.

Both contributions address the design of full-process autonomous AI scientist systems and derive principled guidance for building them. 'Related' is the most defensible classification.

Both contributions demonstrate that multi-agent LLM-based systems can autonomously produce meaningful scientific discoveries, corroborating a shared core finding. Contribution A (BABY-AIGS) shows that a full-process multi-agent system produces meaningful scientific discoveries across diverse tasks (AQ, A:003), while Contribution B (SciAgents) shows that a multi-agent system with specialized roles can reveal hidden interdisciplinary relationships surpassing human methods (BQ, B:000, B:002). The tension is not a direct contradiction on the same construct — A measures output quality relative to human researchers across general tasks, while B focuses on scale and exploratory power in a specific domain (biologically inspired materials). Both contributions demonstrate that multi-agent AI systems can autonomously produce meaningful scientific discoveries. Both contributions address the same high-level challenge — building full-process, multi-agent AI systems capable of autonomous end-to-end scientific discovery — and share structural similarities (multi-agent pipelines, hypothesis formulation, experiment execution, manuscript authoring). Both contributions address the same high-level challenge—building autonomous, full-process AI scientist systems capable of producing meaningful scientific discoveries—and both report quality gaps or gains relative to baselines/humans. Both contributions describe multi-agent AI systems that autonomously conduct or assist with scientific research using LLM-powered agents handling distinct research workflow stages (A: BABY-AIGS with PROPOSALAGENT, EXPAGENT, REVIEWAGENT, FALSIFICATIONAGENT; B: AI co-scientist with Generation, Reflection, Ranking, Evolution, Proximity, Meta-review agents). The structural similarity (multi-agent, iterative refinement) is substantial enough to warrant a 'related' classification, but the lack of citation, the different focal mechanisms (falsification vs. generate-debate-evolve), and no direct evidence of one building on or contradicting the other preclude a harder relation type.

Both contributions demonstrate that multi-agent LLM systems can autonomously execute the full scientific discovery pipeline — including hypothesis generation, experimental design/execution, and iterative refinement — and both report meaningful scientific outputs from their respective systems (AQ: "meaningful scientific discoveries"; BQ: identification of ripasudil for dAMD). However, there is no citation between the papers, no explicit methodological reuse, and the systems are independently constructed with distinct architectures (BABY-AIGS with DSL/falsification phases vs. Robin with Crow/Falcon/Finch agents in a lab-in-the-loop framework). The convergent finding — that end-to-end multi-agent AI can produce real scientific results, albeit with acknowledged limitations relative to human researchers — constitutes comparable corroborating findings, supporting a 'supports' classification, though the type confidence is moderate given that each paper operates in different domains and makes somewhat different claims about quality gaps and autonomy levels.

Both contributions describe multi-agent autonomous AI systems that cover the full scientific research pipeline (idea generation, hypothesis formulation, experiment execution, evaluation, and revision) applied to ML research tasks, and both report partial success with notable limitations. Both contributions independently demonstrate that a fully automated, end-to-end multi-agent AI system can autonomously execute the entire scientific research pipeline — from idea generation through experimentation to manuscript writing — and produce meaningful scientific outputs. Both contributions describe multi-agent AI systems capable of autonomous scientific discovery end-to-end, and both acknowledge a gap relative to human researchers while demonstrating meaningful outputs (BABY-AIGS: scientific discoveries across diverse tasks [AQ, A:003]; Orion: 52 reports and 22 prioritized hypotheses from biological imaging [BQ, B:001]). Both contributions address the same overarching problem domain — AI/LLM assistance in academic peer review — and share a common framing: LLMs should complement rather than replace human reviewers (A:001, B:001, B:002, B:003). Both contributions address LLM-assisted academic peer review — ReviewCritique (A) benchmarks LLMs as reviewers/meta-reviewers via a fine-grained annotated dataset, while AnnotateGPT (B) deploys GPT-4 to assist human reviewers via manuscript annotation highlights. They share the same broad problem domain (AI augmentation of peer review) and both note that LLMs are unsuitable for fully replacing human reviewers (B:001, A:001). However, there is no citation between them, no explicit methodological dependency, and no direct corroboration or contradiction of findings. A does not build on B's platform, and B does not use A's dataset or metrics. The shared domain warrants a 'related' classification, but the evidence does not support a harder relation such as 'builds_on' or 'supports'.

Both contributions independently produce annotated benchmark datasets pairing paper submissions with reviews and LLM-generated outputs to evaluate LLM capabilities in peer review / meta-reviewing contexts. Contribution A (ReviewCritique) provides 100 NLP submissions with sentence-level deficiency annotations for both human and LLM reviews, targeting LLM-as-reviewer and LLM-as-meta-reviewer benchmarking (AQ, A:001, A:002). Contribution B provides 40 ICLR submissions with peer-reviewer comments, expert meta-reviews, and 480 LLM-generated multi-perspective summaries annotated with 4,800 human judgments for evaluating LLM-assisted meta-reviewing (BQ, B:001, B:002, B:009). Their comparable empirical findings — both finding LLMs capable of generating plausible but imperfect review-related content, and both stressing the need for human oversight — materially corroborate one another. There is no citation between them, no evidence that one explicitly builds on or refines the other, but their parallel findings on LLM meta-reviewing capability provide mutual corroboration. The relationship is best characterized as 'supports' (symmetric) rather than 'builds_on' or 'refines', as neither dataset explicitly extends or corrects the other; they converge on the same conclusion through independent designs.

Both contributions address the same broad problem space — using LLMs in academic peer review and evaluating the quality of AI-generated research outputs — and both involve comparing LLM-generated assessments to human expert judgment. Contribution A (ReviewCritique) provides a benchmark dataset with sentence-level deficiency annotations for evaluating LLMs as reviewers and meta-reviewers of NLP papers. Contribution B (MLR-Judge) is an automated LLM-based evaluation framework with structured rubrics validated against human expert reviewers for assessing AI-generated research. There is no citation between the papers in the corpus, and the evidence does not show that B explicitly builds on A's dataset or methods, nor that A's findings are directly extended or corrected by B. The shared thematic focus on LLM-human reviewer agreement and scalable AI peer review evaluation establishes a substantive topical relationship, but the specific methods, artifacts, and findings are distinct enough that no harder relational type (builds_on, supports, refines, contradicts) is defensible from the available evidence alone.

Both contributions independently arrive at the finding that LLM-generated content is less diverse and more generic/predictable than human-written content. Contribution A quantifies this through its ITF-IDF metric for review specificity (A:006), and also observes that LLM-generated reviews are "paper-unspecific and superficial" (A:005). Contribution B similarly finds that LLM-generated research content is less diverse and follows more predictable patterns (BQ). These are comparable, corroborating findings about the same general phenomenon (reduced diversity/specificity in LLM outputs), though in different domains (paper reviews vs. research proposals). There is insufficient evidence to claim one builds on or refines the other.

Both contributions independently characterize a quality gap between LLM-generated and human-written paper reviews, arriving at corroborating findings. Contribution A finds LLM reviews are paper-unspecific, lack diversity, and contain more deficient segments (AQ, A:005). Contribution B finds general-purpose LLMs are insufficiently critical and produce overly positive recommendations compared to human expert reviewers (BQ, B:003, B:020). Specifically, A:005 notes LLMs "tend to accept authors' claims in submissions without much critical evaluation," directly corroborating B's finding that LLMs are "not critical enough." Both converge on the conclusion that LLM reviews are qualitatively inferior to human reviews in distinct but mutually reinforcing ways (lack of criticism/specificity vs. leniency bias). There is no citation between the papers, but the findings materially corroborate each other on the core claim that LLMs fall short of human reviewing quality. The relationship is supports rather than builds_on because neither paper explicitly uses the other's methods or artifacts.

Both contributions independently find that LLM-generated content is less diverse than human-written content: Contribution A demonstrates quantitatively that LLM-generated reviews are less diverse than human reviews (inter-LLM BERTScore 70.33–71.17 vs. inter-human 59.15, [A:009]), and Contribution B finds that LLM-generated research content is less diverse and follows more predictable patterns [BQ]. These are comparable findings on the same construct (lower diversity of LLM outputs relative to humans), supporting one another. However, there is no citation between the papers and the contexts differ (peer reviews vs. research proposals), so the relationship is best characterized as supports rather than a harder type. The evidence is convergent but topically adjacent rather than directly corroborating the same experimental setup.

Both contributions independently arrive at materially compatible findings: general-purpose LLMs, including top closed-source and open-source models, fall significantly short of human expert reviewers in the academic peer-review context. Contribution A demonstrates this in the meta-reviewing task (identifying deficient review segments), finding that even top-tier LLMs struggle to mimic human experts [AQ, A:009, A:011]. Contribution B demonstrates this in the paper-reviewing task, finding that general-purpose LLMs (GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Llama variants) are systematically too lenient and produce recommendation distributions far more positive than human expert reviewers [BQ, B:003, B:012, B:015]. Both converge on the shared finding that current general-purpose LLMs cannot replicate human expert judgment in reviewing tasks. There is no citation link between the papers, and neither explicitly uses or extends the other's methods or artifacts, so builds_on/refines is not defensible. The corroboration of the shared core finding (LLMs fall short of human expert reviewers) is substantive enough to warrant 'supports' rather than merely 'related'.

Both contributions concern the capabilities and limitations of LLMs as imperfect agents relative to human experts. Contribution A empirically demonstrates that LLMs fall short of human expert meta-reviewers in a peer-review context, while Contribution B proposes a theoretical framework for characterizing LLMs as probabilistic imperfect experts along dimensions of reliability, consistency, uncertainty, and content vs. reasoning. There is a substantive thematic overlap — both grapple with LLM imperfection relative to human expertise — but neither explicitly builds on, uses, or cites the other (no citation exists in the corpus), and the findings are neither directly corroborating nor contradictory (they operate in different domains: academic meta-reviewing vs. causal hypothesis generation). The connection is real but not strong enough to classify as supports, builds_on, or refines without overreaching the evidence.

Contribution A finds that even top-tier LLMs substantially fall short of human expert meta-reviewers in assessing the quality of individual paper reviews, concluding that current LLMs cannot replicate the nuanced judgment required (AQ, A:001, A:009). Contribution B (MLR-Judge) finds that an LLM-based judge achieves agreement with human expert reviewers that is statistically indistinguishable from inter-human agreement, concluding that LLMs can serve as reliable proxies for human reviewers in evaluating research quality (BQ, B:022, B:023, B:006). These findings point in opposite directions on the same core construct: whether LLMs can match human expert judgment in peer-review-related tasks. However, the tension is partially mitigated by differences in scope — Contribution A focuses specifically on the meta-reviewing subtask of identifying deficient review segments (a fine-grained, highly expert-demanding classification problem), while Contribution B evaluates overall research quality assessment using structured rubrics across broader dimensions. The tasks are related but not identical, and there is no direct citation between the papers. The divergent conclusions on LLM-vs-human alignment in the reviewing domain constitute a meaningful contradictory signal, though the task-level differences reduce full confidence in classifying this as a hard contradiction.

Both contributions address LLM capability gaps in automated peer review tasks, using evaluations across closed-source and open-source LLMs. Contribution A (ReviewCritique) specifically benchmarks LLMs as meta-reviewers finding they fall short of human experts, while Contribution B (MMReview) evaluates 21 LLMs on a broader multidisciplinary/multimodal benchmark for peer review automation. B cites A, and evidence [B:005] references prior work showing "even advanced models like GPT-4o often fail to meet human expectations in review quality," which aligns with A's findings. However, the citation passage is unavailable, and the two contributions use distinct benchmarks (ReviewCritique vs. MMReview), distinct task scopes (meta-reviewing deficiency detection vs. multi-dimensional peer review tasks), and distinct methodologies. While B builds its context partly on findings like A's, there is no explicit evidence that B directly uses A's dataset, method, or results as a foundation—it cites A as related prior work. The relationship is substantive (both address the same problem space and B acknowledges A's findings) but the evidence is insufficient to firmly classify this as builds_on or supports; related is the most defensible classification.

Both AgentReview (A) and GAR (B) independently develop LLM-agent frameworks that simulate academic peer review, as confirmed by their own descriptions [AQ, BQ, A:001, B:001]. They share the same domain, general methodology (LLM agents enacting reviewer roles), and several overlapping components (e.g., both include a meta-reviewer agent synthesizing individual reviews into a final decision [A:002, B:005]). However, the two contributions are oriented toward distinct goals: AgentReview focuses on controlled disentanglement of latent variables (commitment, intention, knowledgeability, AC behavior) in peer review using simulated data without needing sensitive real-world data [A:001, A:008], while GAR focuses on automating expert-level feedback and predicting acceptance likelihood using real-world reviewer profiles, graph-based manuscript representations, and memory modules [B:004, B:005, B:006]. There is no citation between them, no evidence that either explicitly builds on or extends the other's methods or results, and no directly contradictory empirical findings on the same construct. The relationship is substantive (parallel independent efforts in the same niche) but no harder relation type—such as builds_on, supports, or contradicts—is defensible from the available evidence.

Both contributions operate in the same domain — LLM-agent-based simulation of the academic peer review process — and share structural overlap: both model reviewer characteristics, both generate simulated reviews, and both include a meta-reviewer stage (A:002, A:003, B:005, B:011). However, the contributions are distinct and independently motivated. Contribution A (AgentReview) focuses on a full-pipeline simulation framework for disentangling latent variables such as reviewer commitment, intention, and knowledgeability (A:001, A:002). Contribution B's contrastive-comparison technique focuses on extracting fine-grained reviewer personas (strictness, evidence focus, tone, etc.) from a single historical review to enable faithful replication of individual reviewer styles (BQ, B:018). There is no citation between the papers, and no evidence that either explicitly uses, extends, or corrects the other's methods or results. The persona dimensions in B (strictness, tone, open-mindedness) are conceptually adjacent to but distinct from the reviewer dimensions in A (commitment, intention, knowledgeability), and there is no evidence that one framework's artifact or result was directly adopted by the other. A 'builds_on' or 'refines' label is not defensible without explicit evidence of one acting on the other. The relationship is substantive (same problem space, overlapping design choices) but the hard type cannot be determined from the available evidence, making 'related' the most appropriate classification.

Both contributions address the same problem domain — LLM agent-based simulation of peer review — and share overlapping design goals (multi-phase review pipelines, agent roles, meta-review generation). Contribution A (AgentReview) models a full five-phase peer review pipeline with customizable reviewer/author/AC characteristics for controlled latent-variable disentanglement [A:000, A:002, AQ]. Contribution B (GAR) introduces a multi-round review process with memory retrieval and self-assessment to emulate iterative real-world review [BQ, B:005, B:006, B:023]. However, there is no citation between the papers [citation facts], and neither contribution explicitly uses or extends the other's methods or artifacts. Both independently propose LLM-agent peer review frameworks with overlapping but distinct mechanisms (AgentReview focuses on sociological variable disentanglement; GAR focuses on memory-augmented iterative refinement and graph-based paper representation). The shared design element of multi-phase/multi-round review and meta-reviewer agents [A:002, B:011] establishes a substantive thematic relationship, but there is insufficient evidence to classify this as builds_on, refines, supports, or contradicts. 'Related' is the most defensible classification.

Both contributions independently develop LLM agent-based frameworks that simulate the peer review process, and both include a meta-review/area-chair phase that aggregates individual reviews into a final decision (A:002, A:003, B:024). Contribution A (AgentReview) frames a full simulation pipeline to disentangle latent sociological variables in peer review without needing real-world data. Contribution B (GAR) independently proposes a meta-reviewer agent as part of its own automated review framework. There is no citation between the papers, no evidence that B builds on A's methods or artifacts, and no evidence that A builds on B. The meta-reviewer concept in B (B:024) parallels the AC/meta-review compilation phase in A (A:003), but the implementations and goals differ sufficiently (variable disentanglement vs. prediction accuracy improvement) that 'supports' is not clearly defensible either—A does not compare simulation outcomes to real results (A:008), while B validates against human reviewers. The relationship is substantive (both occupy the same niche of LLM-simulated peer review with a meta-review aggregation step) but no hard semantic type—builds_on, refines, supports, or contradicts—is well-supported by the evidence. 'Related' is the appropriate classification.

Both contributions operate in the domain of computational/automated academic peer review, but they address distinct problems with different artifacts and methods. Contribution A (AgentReview) produces a large-scale *synthetic* peer review corpus (53,800+ documents) generated via LLM agent simulation of the ICLR review process, intended to support research on peer review dynamics. Contribution B (Llama-OpenReviewer-8B) fine-tunes a language model on 79,000 *real* expert reviews from ICLR/NeurIPS to generate structured critical reviews for authors. There is no citation between the papers, and no evidence that B uses A's corpus as training data (B uses real human reviews, not AgentReview's synthetic data) or that A builds on B's model. B:019 references related evaluation and ethics work but not A. The shared topical domain (LLM-assisted peer review, ICLR data) establishes a substantive thematic relationship, but the contributions do not materially corroborate each other's findings, nor does one explicitly use or extend the other. 'Related' is the most defensible classification.

Both contributions document prestige/authority bias corrupting peer review objectivity. Contribution A finds a 27.7% decision shift when author identities are known (human reviewers). Contribution B finds LLMs produce more favorable reviews when authorship is attributed to well-known researchers — the same construct in a different reviewer type. Evidence [B:007] and [CIT:openalex:W4405035007->openalex:W4404783497:3] confirm B's finding directly parallels A's authority-bias result, materially corroborating it. The citation from B to A appears in background motivation context, not as a direct methodological extension, so builds_on is not defensible. Supports is the strongest defensible relation given the analogous but cross-domain (human vs. LLM) nature of the findings.

Both contributions address the intersection of LLMs and academic peer review, specifically the question of how much LLMs can reliably substitute or augment human judgment. Contribution A argues for LLM-generated annotations as a middle ground that complements (but does not replace) human reviewers, noting LLMs' limits in high-level critical thinking (A:001, A:003). Contribution B demonstrates via MLR-Judge that an LLM-based evaluation framework can achieve human-level agreement with expert reviewers, positioning LLMs as a scalable proxy (B:006, B:022, B:023). Their findings point in somewhat different directions—A is cautious about LLM replacement while B is more affirmative about LLM reliability—but neither is directly measuring the same construct or addressing the same specific question (annotation highlights vs. structured rubric-based evaluation of AI-generated papers). There is no citation link between them and no direct methodological dependency. The thematic overlap is substantive (both concern LLM roles in review), but no hard semantic relation (supports, builds_on, refines, contradicts) is defensible from the evidence alone.

Both contributions independently document that general-purpose LLMs are insufficiently critical as peer reviewers. A finds hallucination and prestige bias as inherent flaws; B finds LLMs are systematically too lenient (more positive recommendations than humans). These are corroborating, compatible findings about the same construct (LLM reviewer quality deficiencies). B cites A in an ethics/bias context [CIT], and B's evidence [B:003] that 'general-purpose LLMs are not critical enough and tend to give much more positive recommendations than human reviews' materially corroborates A's finding that LLMs have inherent flaws compromising review objectivity. The relationship is supports (symmetric) rather than builds_on because B does not explicitly use A's method or artifact—it independently evaluates different LLMs with a different approach (fine-tuning comparison), and the citation is background rather than methodological extension.

Both contributions address LLM limitations — Contribution A empirically documents specific flaws (hallucination, prestige bias) in scholarly peer review, while Contribution B proposes a conceptual framework for characterizing LLMs as probabilistic imperfect experts along dimensions including reliability, consistency, uncertainty, and hallucination. There is thematic overlap: B:028 discusses hallucination as a dimension of LLM characterization, which is also central to A's findings (A:031, A:007), and B:039 raises concerns about naive LLM use in science that resonates with A's conclusions. However, there is no citation between the papers, no evidence that either work explicitly builds on, refines, or uses the other's methods or results. The shared concern about LLM flaws is at a topical/background level rather than a direct contribution-level relationship. 'Related' is the most defensible classification given the substantive thematic connection without a demonstrable hard semantic link.

Both contributions address the same core problem — automating academic peer review with LLMs — and arrive at compatible, mutually reinforcing findings. Contribution A (GAR) demonstrates that LLM-based agents can produce reviews that "align closely with human reviewers" (A:041), including on score distributions. Contribution B (OpenReviewer) demonstrates that general-purpose LLMs (GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet) are systematically too lenient and that specialized fine-tuning is needed to match human reviewer distributions (B:015, B:001, BQ). These findings are coherent: A's result that a carefully designed LLM-agent framework can approximate human review quality corroborates B's finding that off-the-shelf LLMs alone are insufficient but that targeted approaches can close the gap. There is no citation between the papers, and neither explicitly builds on the other's methodology or artifacts. The relationship is best characterized as supports (comparable findings corroborating each other) rather than a directional builds_on or refines, though confidence in the exact type is moderate given the different technical approaches (agent architecture vs. fine-tuning) and the lack of cross-citation.

Both contributions independently arrive at the same core empirical finding: LLM-based reviewers can achieve agreement with human expert reviewers that is comparable to inter-human agreement. GAR (Contribution A) demonstrates high correlation between LLM-agent scores and human reviewer scores across criteria such as soundness and presentation (A:041), and uses GPT-4o to confirm human-likeness of generated reviews. MLR-Judge (Contribution B) conducts a formal Mann-Whitney U significance test showing that LLM-human score differences are not statistically larger than human-human differences across five criteria (B:022, B:023, B:006). These are parallel, corroborating findings on the same construct (LLM reviewer alignment with human experts), supporting a 'supports' relation. However, the papers do not cite each other, address somewhat different scopes (GAR focuses on automating peer review of submitted papers; MLR-Judge focuses on evaluating AI-generated research quality), and use different methodologies and benchmarks, so the relation is supportive rather than a harder build_on or refines. The type confidence is moderate because the topical overlap is strong but the specific constructs and experimental setups differ enough that the corroboration is partial rather than direct.

Both contributions address LLM-based automated peer review with human alignment as a core validation goal. Contribution A (GAR) proposes a meta-reviewer agent that aggregates individual LLM-generated reviews into a final decision, and validates that its outputs correlate strongly with human reviewers (A:041, A:006). Contribution B (MLR-Judge) introduces a rubric-based LLM judge and demonstrates statistically that its agreement with human reviewers is comparable to inter-human agreement (B:022, B:023, B:006, B:029). Both share the overarching theme of LLM-as-reviewer with human-alignment validation, which is a substantive topical and methodological overlap. However, there is no citation between the papers, no explicit reuse or extension of each other's methods or artifacts, and no directly comparable finding on the same construct that would constitute supports or contradicts. A's meta-reviewer agent is a distinct architectural contribution (aggregation of synthetic reviews for acceptance prediction), while B's MLR-Judge is an evaluation framework for AI-generated research quality—related but not directly building on or refining one another. 'Related' is the most defensible classification given the shared domain and parallel human-alignment validation without a harder demonstrable link.

Both contributions independently arrive at structurally similar and mutually corroborating findings: (1) an ensemble of individual LLM-generated reviews is aggregated by a meta-reviewer/area-chair agent into a single final acceptance decision, and (2) this approach achieves accuracy comparable to human reviewers when validated against real conference data (e.g., ICLR, OpenReview). Contribution A (GAR) proposes a meta-reviewer agent that synthesizes individual reviews into a final decision and demonstrates improved prediction accuracy (A:024, AQ). Contribution B (Automated Reviewer) independently implements the same architectural pattern—five independent reviews aggregated by an LLM acting as area chair—and validates it against human decisions at ICLR/NeurIPS, achieving human-level accuracy (B:008, B:002, BQ). The core empirical findings are comparable: LLM-based ensemble review with a meta-reviewer layer can replicate collective human judgment. There is no citation between them, but the findings materially corroborate each other. The relationship is supports rather than builds_on because there is no evidence either paper explicitly uses or extends the other's method or artifacts.

MLR-Judge (B) explicitly cites OpenReviewer (A) as prior work in the LLM-as-reviewer space, noting its limitations (overconfident, unreliable overall judgments), then builds on those insights by introducing a more structured rubric-based approach. Evidence CIT:2 and B:029 show B directly frames MLR-Judge as building on lessons from A and similar works. This is a builds_on relation with B acting on A.

Both contributions concern LLM capabilities and limitations: Contribution A empirically demonstrates that general-purpose LLMs are overly lenient as peer reviewers and that fine-tuning closes this gap, while Contribution B proposes a theoretical framework for characterizing LLMs as probabilistic imperfect experts along dimensions like reliability, consistency, and uncertainty. There is a conceptual overlap — A's finding that LLMs are systematically biased (over-positive) is thematically relevant to B's framework for characterizing LLM imperfections. However, there is no citation between the papers, A does not use or extend B's framework, and B does not build on A's empirical findings. The relationship is substantive at a topical level (both address LLM imperfection/characterization) but no hard relation such as builds_on, supports, or refines is defensible from the evidence: A's domain is peer review quality/fine-tuning, B's domain is causal hypothesis generation. The shared theme of LLM imperfection is insufficient to establish a stronger link.

Both SciAgents and SciSciGPT are multi-agent LLM-based frameworks designed to automate scientific research workflows, and both employ prompt engineering and role specialization across agents. However, the two systems are distinct in focus and architecture: SciAgents centers on ontological knowledge graphs for hypothesis generation in bioinspired materials (AQ, A:000, A:002), while SciSciGPT targets empirical workflows in the science of science domain with a hierarchical five-agent structure for data extraction, analytics, and reproducibility (BQ, B:001, B:003). There is no citation between them in the corpus, and no evidence that one explicitly builds on, uses, or refines the other's methods or results. Their shared use of multi-agent LLM architectures and prompt engineering establishes a substantive topical relationship, but this alone is insufficient to support a harder relation type such as builds_on or supports without material corroboration of findings or explicit methodological extension.

Both contributions address automated scientific hypothesis generation using knowledge graphs, LLMs, and ontologies, placing them firmly in the same problem space. Contribution A (SciAgents) uses sub-graph sampling from large ontological knowledge graphs to contextualize multi-agent hypothesis generation (AQ, A:002, A:003). Contribution B uses inductive logic programming combined with LLMs and rigorous ontologies grounded in community databases to generate and validate hypotheses with reduced hallucination (BQ, B:001, B:006, B:007). There are meaningful thematic overlaps: both use graph databases, ontologies, LLMs, and multi-agent or automated reasoning pipelines for scientific discovery. However, there is no citation link between the papers, no evidence that one explicitly builds on or uses the other's methods or artifacts, and the specific technical mechanisms differ substantially (sub-graph path sampling for in-context LLM reasoning in A, vs. inductive logic programming + supervised learning + LLM experimental design in B). The overlap is substantive enough to preclude 'none', but not specific enough to justify builds_on, refines, supports, or contradicts. 'Related' is the most defensible classification.

Both contributions operate at the intersection of knowledge graph-based representations, LLMs, and automated scientific hypothesis generation, establishing a substantive topical relationship. Contribution A (SciAgents) uses sub-graph sampling from large ontological knowledge graphs to guide multi-agent hypothesis generation (AQ, A:000, A:002, A:003). Contribution B uses description logic-based representation of hypotheses and stores experimental data in a graph database using controlled vocabularies and extended ontologies (BQ, B:001, B:005, B:006, B:007). However, the two contributions are technically and methodologically distinct: A focuses on sampling strategies over large pre-built knowledge graphs to contextualize LLM-driven multi-agent reasoning, while B focuses on formal logical representation and automated capture of hypotheses, protocols, and empirical data in a structured database using ontologies and inductive logic programming. There is no citation between them, no evidence that one builds directly on the other's method or result, no shared dataset or construct being tested for compatibility, and no refining relationship. The overlap is at a high level (knowledge graphs + LLMs + hypothesis generation), but the specific contributions do not materially corroborate, extend, or contradict each other. 'Related' is the most defensible classification.

Both contributions sit at the intersection of LLM-driven agents and knowledge graphs for scientific automation, but they address distinctly different problems with different architectures. Contribution A (SciAgents) introduces a sub-graph sampling strategy over large ontological knowledge graphs to contextualize multi-agent hypothesis generation in materials science (evidenced by AQ, A:002, A:003). Contribution B (El Agente Gráfico) uses a single-agent framework with typed execution graphs and knowledge-graph persistence for scientific computation, managing context through typed symbolic identifiers (evidenced by BQ, B:002, B:007). The knowledge graphs in A are ontological/semantic and used for subgraph sampling to seed reasoning, while in B they serve as a typed runtime state store for a computational workflow — these are functionally and architecturally distinct uses. There is no citation between the papers, no explicit building-on, refinement, or direct contradiction of findings. The shared surface-level vocabulary (knowledge graphs, LLMs, scientific automation) establishes topical similarity but not a hard contribution-level relationship. 'Related' is the most defensible classification.

Both contributions address the same problem space—combining LLMs with other knowledge sources (experts, logic-based methods, data-driven approaches) for scientific hypothesis generation—and share key concerns about hallucination mitigation and the integration of structured knowledge. Contribution A proposes a conceptual spectrum of integration methods for experts, LLMs, and data-driven causal hypothesis generation [AQ, A:006, A:005]. Contribution B instantiates a hybrid pipeline using ILP, LLMs, and ontologies grounded in community databases for biological hypothesis generation, explicitly motivated by the need to combine rigor with LLM flexibility [B:004, B:005, BQ]. However, there is no citation link between the papers, B does not explicitly build on or extend A's framework, and A does not refine or correct B. The overlap is topical and conceptual rather than a direct methodological dependency or corroboration of specific findings. The relationship is substantive but not hard-typed as builds_on, supports, or refines.

Both contributions address the same problem space — integrating LLMs, data-driven methods, and knowledge sources for causal/scientific hypothesis generation — and share overlapping constructs. Contribution A (a perspective/review paper) proposes a conceptual spectrum of integration methods ranging from purely data-driven to purely knowledge-driven and calls for benchmarks enabling comparison across this spectrum [A:006, A:005, AQ]. Contribution B operationalizes a closely related idea by empirically comparing six hypothesis-generation methods (including data-driven, literature-augmented, and zero/few-shot LLM approaches) across four LLMs, finding that Literature+Data (a hybrid approach sitting in A's spectrum) performs best [BQ, B:006, B:019, B:005]. There is no citation link between the papers, and B does not explicitly cite or extend A's framework. However, B's benchmark design and method taxonomy are conceptually aligned with the spectrum A proposes, and B's finding that hybrid (Literature+Data) methods outperform purely data-driven or purely knowledge-driven ones is consistent with A's advocacy for integration. This is insufficient to classify as 'builds_on' (no explicit use of A's artifact/framework by B) or 'supports' (the contributions are not directly comparable empirical findings). The relationship is substantive but best characterized as 'related'.

Both contributions are substantively concerned with characterizing the reliability and limitations of LLMs as evaluators/experts. Contribution A formalizes LLMs as probabilistic imperfect experts along dimensions including reliability, consistency, and uncertainty [AQ, A:001, A:003], while Contribution B empirically demonstrates that LLM-as-judge scores are unreliable relative to expert ratings for scientific ideation tasks, explicitly quantifying variation between automated and expert evaluation [BQ, B:003, B:007]. These are thematically related — both address the trustworthiness and calibration of LLM outputs relative to human expert judgment — but there is no citation link between the papers, no evidence that B builds on or uses A's framework, and no evidence that A's framework directly informs or is tested by B's empirical findings. The relationship is substantive (shared concern with LLM reliability and expert comparison) but no hard type (builds_on, refines, supports, contradicts) is defensible from the evidence: A is a framework paper focused on causal hypothesis generation, while B is an empirical evaluation study for scientific ideation. They converge thematically but do not directly corroborate, extend, or contradict each other's specific findings.

B (W7149942558) explicitly cites A (W4407632372) and positions A's always-valid e-process gates as a component that maps into B's declared inferential checker families with seal nodes. Evidence B:011 states 'always-valid e-process gates map to declared inferential checker families with seal nodes' and describes A as a 'concrete protocol-level instantiation' that B's architecture generalizes. CIT passage confirms B treats A's framework as an essential substrate that B incorporates and extends into a broader certification-and-release governance architecture. This is builds_on with direction b_to_a (B builds on A).

Both contributions address automated hypothesis validation in biological systems using LLM-based agentic frameworks. Contribution A (POPPER) proposes a sequential falsification framework with strict Type-I error control, benchmarked against human PhD-level scientists at 10× speed. Contribution B presents a self-driven biological discovery pipeline integrating LLMs, relational learning, and automated laboratory infrastructure (robotics, metabolomics) to generate and validate hypotheses in S. cerevisiae, yielding novel biological findings. The two systems share the same high-level goal (automated hypothesis validation in biology with LLMs) and operate in overlapping scientific territory, but there is no citation between them, no explicit methodological dependency, and no direct comparison or use of each other's artifacts. Contribution B's specific biological findings (glutamate/spermine, aminoadipate/formic acid) are empirical outputs of its own pipeline rather than a validation or extension of POPPER. The relationship is substantive (same research agenda, same domain) but does not rise to builds_on, refines, supports, or contradicts given the lack of direct engagement between the two works.

Both AIDE (Contribution A) and MLGym (Contribution B) operate in the same problem space — LLM agents tackling ML/AI research tasks — but serve distinct purposes. AIDE is a concrete tree-search-based code optimization agent for ML engineering, while MLGym is a Gym-compatible environment and evaluation framework for developing and benchmarking LLM agents on AI research tasks. There is no citation between the two papers, and neither paper explicitly uses, extends, or evaluates the other's artifact or methodology. However, a substantive thematic relationship exists: MLGym is designed to host and evaluate agents like AIDE, and AIDE's approach is representative of the class of agents MLGym targets. Evidence [A:026] notes AIDE generalizes to "AI R&D tasks," and [B:006]/[B:007] describe MLGym as a platform for evaluating LLM agents on open-ended AI research tasks across diverse domains. This overlap is topical and architectural rather than a direct build-on or supports relationship, as neither paper materially corroborates or extends the other's findings. The absence of citation further limits the defensible relation to 'related'.

AI Scientist-v2 (B) explicitly states it was 'inspired by' AIDE's tree-search approach and integrates 'a similar tree search-based exploration strategy' adapted to scientific experimentation. Evidence B:003 and CIT:2 directly describe adopting AIDE's methodology — each node as a solution state with scalar evaluation scores — into their framework, constituting a clear builds_on relationship from B to A.

AIDE (Contribution A) and AlphaEvolve (Contribution B) share a substantively overlapping design paradigm: both are LLM-powered coding agents that iteratively improve code/algorithms guided by automated evaluation metrics. AIDE frames ML engineering as a tree search over Python solutions using draft/debug/improve operators [AQ, A:006], while AlphaEvolve uses evolutionary computation over full code files guided by automated evaluators [BQ, B:000, B:004]. The papers do not cite each other (no citation in the corpus graph), and there is no evidence that either explicitly builds on, refines, or contradicts the other's methods or findings. AlphaEvolve's related-work discussion [B:046] cites comparable LLM-guided evolution systems but does not mention AIDE. The shared architectural motif (LLM + automated evaluation + iterative code improvement) establishes a clear substantive relationship, but the absence of direct engagement between the two works, and the fact that they target somewhat different problem domains (ML engineering benchmarks vs. open scientific/algorithmic discovery), prevents classification as supports, builds_on, or refines. 'Related' is the most defensible classification.

Both contributions share a structurally similar paradigm: iterative LLM-driven code improvement guided by automated evaluation metrics, organized as a search over a space of executable programs. AIDE (A) uses a solution tree where nodes are standalone scripts and a hard-coded policy governs drafting/debugging/improving [A:006, A:007, A:008]. AlphaEvolve (B) uses an evolutionary approach with a pool of algorithms, LLM-based code edits, and automated evaluators [B:000, B:002, B:004]. However, there is no citation between the papers in the corpus [citation facts], and B does not explicitly build on or reference AIDE's tree structure or policy. B's comparison table [B:004] references FunSearch as its predecessor, not AIDE. The shared conceptual territory (LLM + automated eval + iterative code improvement) is substantive, but the evidence does not support a harder relation (builds_on/refines) — the architectural choices differ (tree search with hard-coded policy vs. evolutionary population-based approach), and no explicit extension or correction relationship is evidenced. 'Related' is the most defensible classification.

Both contributions employ LLM-driven iterative code generation and search to discover or optimize solutions: AIDE (A) organizes solutions in a tree structure where nodes are standalone executable scripts and edges represent improvement attempts, targeting ML engineering tasks [A:006, A:007]; AlphaEvolve (B) uses an evolutionary pool of programs guided by LLMs to discover provably better mathematical constructions [B:002, B:015, B:028, B:031]. They share the same high-level paradigm — LLM-generated code evaluated by an automated objective function, with history informing subsequent proposals — but differ in architecture (tree search vs. evolutionary population), domain (ML engineering vs. open mathematical problems), and specific mechanisms. There is no citation between them in the corpus, and neither paper explicitly builds on or refines the other's method or results. Both contributions assess LLMs' capacity for novel research generation, and their findings are in tension. Contribution A (MLGym) finds that frontier LLMs (Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Llama-3.1 405B, GPT-4o, o1-preview, Gemini-1.5 Pro) "do not generate novel hypotheses, algorithms, architectures, or substantial improvements" on open-ended AI research tasks (AQ, A:002). While the tasks differ (A focuses on executable AI research tasks requiring experimentation; B focuses on generating textual future research ideas from papers), both address the same core construct—whether LLMs can produce novel research contributions—and arrive at materially incompatible conclusions: A denies novelty, B affirms it (to a meaningful degree). The overlap in models evaluated (e.g., GPT-4, Gemini variants) strengthens the case for genuine conflict rather than mere topical similarity. The methodological differences (benchmark execution vs. idea generation evaluation) temper confidence in the contradiction type somewhat, as the construct is not perfectly identical.

Both contributions address the limitations of frontier LLMs in scientific discovery tasks and converge on the implication that current general-purpose LLMs are insufficient for higher-order scientific creativity. The relationship is substantive but not hard-typed as supports (the findings are complementary but measured on different constructs/tasks), builds_on, or refines.

Both contributions address the same broad problem space — building LLM-based multi-agent systems that autonomously plan, code, and execute complex biomedical tasks by integrating diverse bioinformatics tools into workflows. Both contributions describe LLM-based agentic frameworks for autonomous biomedical research that integrate specialized bioinformatics tools into executable workflows, plan and execute complex tasks from natural-language prompts, and avoid rigid pre-defined workflows. 'Related' best captures the substantive parallel relationship without overstating the dependency.

Both contributions describe LLM-based generalist agent architectures designed for complex, multi-step task execution in scientific domains, sharing core design motifs: LLM reasoning cores, hierarchical/modular planning, dynamic tool/resource retrieval, and code-based or action-space execution without rigid predefined workflows. 'Related' is the most defensible classification.

Both contributions describe LLM-based agentic architectures that use code as an execution interface to enable dynamic, flexible composition of computational workflows without predefined templates. Both contributions address the same core problem: enabling LLM-based agents to autonomously plan, code, and execute complex, multi-step biomedical workflows by integrating diverse bioinformatics tools — without requiring predefined templates or rigid pipelines. Both contributions address the same architectural challenge — enabling agentic AI systems to dynamically integrate tools and compose complex workflows without rigid, predefined templates or hard-coded agent hierarchies — and both use LLM-based reasoning as the core orchestration mechanism. Contribution A (Biomni) achieves this in the biomedical domain via retrieval-augmented planning and code-based execution (AQ, A:011, A:012), while Contribution B (QUASAR) achieves this in computational chemistry via a modular, extensible architecture that lowers the barrier to tool integration (BQ, B:008, B:005, B:028). Both contributions address automated scientific discovery using LLM-driven approaches: Contribution A (Biomni) is a generalist biomedical AI agent that autonomously generates experimentally testable protocols from multi-modal biomedical datasets (AQ, A:002, A:006), while Contribution B presents an automated pipeline integrating LLM-driven experimental design with physical robotic laboratory infrastructure for hypothesis generation and validation in yeast biology (BQ, B:001, B:005, B:006, B:007). Both contributions share a common thematic space: LLM-driven, agentic AI systems for autonomous biological protocol generation and optimization. Both contributions share the same high-level concept—integrating LLMs into iterative experimental workflows for biological hypothesis generation and validation—but operate on distinct biological systems (breast cancer drug combinations vs. S. cerevisiae systems biology), use different automation architectures (human-in-the-loop wet-lab vs. fully robotic pipeline with metabolomics), and there is no citation between the papers. The shared thematic space (LLM-driven scientific discovery with empirical validation) is substantive enough to warrant 'related', but the methodological, biological, and evidential gaps preclude a harder relation type such as supports, builds_on, or refines.

Both contributions share the same high-level empirical claim: that LLM-driven hypothesis generation, when coupled with wet-lab validation, yields actionable drug candidates against cancer. Contribution A demonstrates this via an iterative human–LLM–lab loop for breast cancer drug combinations, showing improved synergy hit rates (AQ, A:002). Contribution B demonstrates this via an AI co-scientist system that proposes AML repurposing candidates subsequently validated in vitro at clinically relevant concentrations (BQ, B:009, B:008, B:013). The findings are parallel and mutually corroborating: both show that AI-generated hypotheses survive empirical wet-lab testing and produce actionable oncology candidates. However, there is no citation between the papers, no explicit methodological reuse, and their scopes differ (drug combinations vs. drug repurposing; breast cancer vs. AML), so a hard builds_on or refines relationship is not defensible. The parallel positive in vitro validation results materially corroborate the shared central claim, supporting a 'supports' relation. The absence of citation and the distinct methodological frameworks (iterative GPT-4 querying vs. multi-agent co-scientist system) preclude a stronger structural relationship.

Both contributions share the core finding that AI/LLM-driven hypothesis generation, coupled with iterative empirical feedback and wet-lab validation, can yield experimentally confirmed scientific discoveries in biomedical research. Contribution A demonstrates that an iterative human–LLM–laboratory loop improves the yield of synergistic drug-combination hits in cancer (AQ, A:001, A:006), while Contribution B demonstrates that a multi-agent AI system can propose novel epigenetic targets for liver fibrosis that are validated in human hepatic organoids (BQ, B:002, B:003, B:013). However, the two contributions operate in distinct disease domains (breast cancer vs. liver fibrosis), use different AI architectures (single LLM vs. multi-agent system), and do not cite each other, so the support is substantive but not tightly coupled. No direct builds_on or refines relationship is established, as neither explicitly uses or extends the other's methods or results. The relation is best classified as 'supports' given the materially corroborating findings about the efficacy of AI-in-the-loop scientific discovery workflows.

Both contributions share a common high-level theme: using LLMs in iterative, empirically-grounded biological workflows to improve scientific outcomes — Contribution A in cancer drug-combination discovery (iterative LLM-wet-lab hypothesis refinement) and Contribution B in autonomous biological protocol optimization (LLM-driven differentiation protocol optimization). Both ACCELMAT and MLR-Agent are LLM-based agentic frameworks designed to automate scientific research workflows — ACCELMAT targets materials discovery hypothesis generation (AQ, A:001, A:002) while MLR-Agent targets open-ended ML research tasks through four sequential stages (BQ, B:001, B:009). Both ACCELMAT (Contribution A) and The AI Scientist-v2 (Contribution B) are LLM-based agentic frameworks for automated scientific discovery that share high-level architectural similarities: iterative hypothesis generation, multi-agent critique/feedback loops, and evaluation components. Evidence B:000 and B:002 describe The AI Scientist-v2 as building on its own predecessor (v1, Lu et al., 2024) without referencing ACCELMAT. There is no evidence of one explicitly using, extending, or correcting the other's methods or results, nor of directly comparable findings that could constitute support or contradiction.
